## Claims

### C-V1R6-01 — Narrative problem: promise vs Sarai’s barrenness
**Targets:** [[genesis]], [[abraham]], [[sarah]], [[hamilton-genesis-1-17-nicot]]  
**Claim (attributed to Hamilton):** Gen 16 opens against ch. 15’s promise of descendant(s); the obstacle is Sarai’s inability to conceive (cf. 11:30). Parallel issue to 12:10ff.: what good are promises if Sarai is dead or her womb is dead? For at least ten years (16:3) they have been childless; Hagar’s presence (cf. 12:16) opens the following narrative.  
**Quote:** “The preceding chapter of Genesis had several references to God’s promise to Abram that he would have both a descendant (v. 4) and descendants (vv. 5, 13, 18). The problem with that possibility ever becoming reality is Sarai’s inability to conceive (see 11:30).”  
**Locus:** L37–L38

### C-V1R6-02 — Sarai attributes barrenness to Yahweh without moral analysis
**Targets:** [[sarah]], [[genesis]], [[hamilton-genesis-1-17-nicot]]  
**Claim (Hamilton):** No reason is given for barrenness beyond that Yahweh has restrained (*ʿāṣar*) her from conceiving (same verb in 20:18 of Philistine women closed for Abimelech’s taking of Sarah—there a sign of divine displeasure). Gen 16:2 makes no such moral claim (nor 1 Sam 1:5 for Hannah). Sarai’s words reflect an OT perspective that Yahweh is ultimate source of life’s experiences; moral analysis is usually not required.  
**Quote:** “Gen. 16:2 makes no such statement… Rather, Sarai’s words reflect an OT perspective that Yahweh is the ultimate source behind all of life’s experiences… And in most cases moral analysis is not required.”  
**Locus:** L42–L43

### C-V1R6-03 — Hagar never named by Sarai/Abram in 16:1–6 (label only)
**Targets:** [[sarah]], [[ishmael]], [[abraham]], [[hamilton-genesis-1-17-nicot]]  
**Claim (Hamilton):** Sarai never addresses or talks of Hagar by name, only by role (“my maidservant”; also v. 5); Abram also avoids her name (v. 6).  
**Quote:** “Sarai never addresses or talks of Hagar by name, but only by label or role, my maidservant (see also v. 5; even Abram avoids her name, v. 6).”  
**Locus:** L44

### C-V1R6-04 — ANE surrogacy parallels; dating caution (Van Seters)
**Targets:** [[genesis]], [[sarah]], [[hamilton-genesis-1-17-nicot]], [[documentary-hypothesis]]  
**Claim (Hamilton):** Four extrabiblical texts illustrate infertile wife procuring a surrogate maidservant: Hammurapi §146; a Nuzi text (Gilimninu/Shennima); Old Assyrian marriage contract (Laqipum/Hatala); Neo-Assyrian text (Ṣubetu). First three 2nd millennium; last 1st millennium. Marriage customs are conservative/long-lived; impossible on archaeology alone to date Gen 16 to 2nd or 1st millennium. Hamilton credits Van Seters for warning against selective second-millennium data for patriarchal dating.  
**Quote:** “It is impossible, simply on the basis of archeology, to date Gen. 16 to either the 2nd or the 1st millennium. We are dealing here with marriage customs which by their very nature are conservative and long-lived.”  
**Locus:** L46–L62

### C-V1R6-05 — Surrogacy as obligation not ignominy (Hamilton’s inclination)
**Targets:** [[sarah]], [[genesis]], [[hamilton-genesis-1-17-nicot]]  
**Claim (Hamilton):** Options: remain barren or present Hagar. Ambiguous whether obligation or privilege; given emphasis on male progeny to perpetuate the line, Hamilton is “inclined to think that Sarai’s action was obligatory, and that no ignominy was attached to such a procedure.”  
**Quote:** “I am inclined to think that Sarai’s action was obligatory, and that no ignominy was attached to such a procedure.”  
**Locus:** L64

### C-V1R6-06 — *pilegeš* and *ʾiššâ*: concubine-wife in Genesis only
**Targets:** [[genesis]], [[abraham]], [[ishmael]], [[hamilton-genesis-1-17-nicot]]  
**Claim (Hamilton):** Outside Genesis, *pilegeš* and *ʾiššâ* are distinct. In Genesis three partners are styled both: Keturah (1 Chr 1:32 *pilegeš* / Gen 25:1 *ʾiššâ*); Hagar (16:3 *ʾiššâ* / 25:6 *pilegeš* with Keturah); Bilhah (35:22 *pilegeš* / 30:4, 37:2 *ʾiššâ*). Suggests patriarchal concubines were not *pilagšîm* in the later sense; terms used as synonyms for that type of concubinage.  
**Quote:** “Unlike the rest of the OT, where women are either wives or concubines, in Genesis we have three instances (Hagar, Keturah, and Bilhah) of a concubine-wife.”  
**Locus:** L66–L68

### C-V1R6-07 — Role reversal: Sarai gives Hagar as Abram once gave Sarai
**Targets:** [[abraham]], [[sarah]], [[genesis]], [[hamilton-genesis-1-17-nicot]]  
**Claim (Hamilton):** Just as Abram gave Sarai to Pharaoh, Sarai gives Hagar to Abram—donor becomes receiver; pawn becomes initiator. Hagar is “taken” then “given,” an instrument without choice; after a decade in Canaan.  
**Quote:** “Just as Abram gave Sarai to Pharaoh, now Sarai gives Hagar to Abram. Abram the donor becomes Abram the receiver, and Sarai the pawn becomes Sarai the initiator. Hagar has no choice in the matter.”  
**Locus:** L70

### C-V1R6-08 — Initiative to force promise; companionship displaced by reproduction
**Targets:** [[sarah]], [[covenant]], [[genesis]], [[hamilton-genesis-1-17-nicot]]  
**Claim (Hamilton):** Story illustrates a child of God pressed to take initiative to bring God’s promises to pass; also replacing marriage’s primary purpose of companionship (Gen 2:18) with reproduction and negative effects.  
**Quote:** “The account provides another illustration of how a child of God, with his or her back to the wall, feels pressed to take the initiative in order to bring God’s promises to pass. … This story also reflects the replacing of marriage’s primary purpose of companionship (Gen. 2:18) by that of reproduction, with all the resulting negative effects.”  
**Locus:** L72

### C-V1R6-09 — Hagar’s pregnancy: pride/equality, not barbs (Hammurapi parallel)
**Targets:** [[ishmael]], [[sarah]], [[hamilton-genesis-1-17-nicot]]  
**Claim (Hamilton):** Hagar conceives easily; no emotional description of Abram’s act. She turns prideful (Sarai’s perception). Hamilton links Hagar’s judgment (v. 4b) to Hammurapi’s “claimed equality with her mistress,” not contempt/insults. Sarai is non-child-producing *ʾiššâ*; Hagar is child-producing *ʾiššâ*—that annoys Sarai. Contrast Bilhah/Zilpah: little tension because already family gifts, whereas Hagar is Egyptian alien.  
**Quote:** “Sarai is now a non-child-producing ʾiššâ, and Hagar is a child-producing ʾiššâ. And that is what annoys Sarai and not any barbs that Hagar is throwing at her.”  
**Locus:** L74

### C-V1R6-10 — Sternberg on narrator/Sarai repetition; Hamilton’s caveat
**Targets:** [[sarah]], [[hamilton-genesis-1-17-nicot]]  
**Claim (Hamilton):** Sternberg notes same formulation of Hagar’s evaluation in narrator (v. 4) and Sarai (v. 5); suggests equivalence legitimates the aggrieved party’s vision. Hamilton: “perhaps Sternberg is reading too much of a denigrating nuance into Sarai’s words.”  
**Quote:** “But perhaps Sternberg is reading too much of a denigrating nuance into Sarai’s words.”  
**Locus:** L76

### C-V1R6-11 — Abram’s false neutrality; defendant then judge
**Targets:** [[abraham]], [[sarah]], [[hamilton-genesis-1-17-nicot]]  
**Claim (Hamilton):** If Hagar shows pride and Sarai false blame, Abram shows “false neutrality”; he too uses label only (“your maidservant” / “her”). V. 5 casts him as defendant; v. 6a as judge; judgment “lame and passive.”  
**Quote:** “If Hagar shows some pride, and if Sarai shows a false blame, Abram demonstrates a false neutrality. … Abram’s judgment on the matter is, at best, lame and passive.”  
**Locus:** L78

### C-V1R6-12 — Exodus parallel with reversed oppressor/oppressed
**Targets:** [[sarah]], [[ishmael]], [[genesis]], [[hamilton-genesis-1-17-nicot]]  
**Claim (Hamilton):** Sarai’s abuse of Hagar (*ʿānâ* III) forcing flight (*bāraḥ*) parallels Egypt’s oppression of Hebrews (*ʿānâ* Gen 15:13; Exod 1:11–12) and flight (*bāraḥ* Exod 14:5), but roles reverse: matriarch of Israel oppresses an Egyptian. Prov 30:21–23 uses same *šiḥâ* / *geḇirtāh* pair as Gen 16.  
**Quote:** “But in Gen. 16 the roles of oppressor and oppressed are just the opposite from Exodus. Here it is a matriarch of Israel oppressing an Egyptian.”  
**Locus:** L80–L82

### C-V1R6-13 — Angel of Yahweh: representation not dilution of theophany
**Targets:** [[genesis]], [[hamilton-genesis-1-17-nicot]]  
**Claim (Hamilton):** Rejects older view (e.g. Gunkel) that angel of Yahweh mitigates/dilutes direct theophany—introduction is too spasmodic and leaves anthropomorphisms. Better: angel is accompaniment of deity’s anthropomorphic appearance, not dilution. Surveys Gen 16; 21:17; 22; 31; Exod 3; Num 22–24; Judg 6; Judg 13: angel both equated with and dissociated from deity.  
**Quote:** “It is better to say that the angel is the accompaniment of the deity’s anthropomorphic appearance, rather than being a dilution of it.”  
**Locus:** L141–L143

### C-V1R6-14 — Angel of Yahweh: more representation than representative (North)
**Targets:** [[genesis]], [[hamilton-genesis-1-17-nicot]]  
**Claim (Hamilton):** Angel of Yahweh is visible manifestation (human or fiery form) essentially indistinguishable from Yahweh; more representation of God than representative. Cites R. North: *malʾāk* means representation/presence rather than messenger as specific form.  
**Quote:** “the angel of Yahweh is a visible manifestation (either in human form or in fiery form) of Yahweh that is essentially indistinguishable from Yahweh himself. The angel of Yahweh is more a representation of God than a representative of God.”  
**Locus:** L147

### C-V1R6-15 — Divine *māṣāʾ* of persons = encounter/election by search
**Targets:** [[ishmael]], [[genesis]], [[hamilton-genesis-1-17-nicot]]  
**Claim (Hamilton):** When God is subject of *māṣāʾ* with personal object, the verb “carries a technical meaning… elements of encounter and, of divine election” (cf. Deut 32:10; Hos 9:10; Ps 89:21)—find by search, not stumble.  
**Quote:** “when God is the subject of māṣāʾ, and the following object is personal, māṣāʾ ‘carries a technical meaning going well beyond connotations of the English verb: it includes elements of encounter and, of divine election.’”  
**Locus:** L151

### C-V1R6-16 — Angel knows Hagar; she answers only “from where”
**Targets:** [[ishmael]], [[sarah]], [[hamilton-genesis-1-17-nicot]]  
**Claim (Hamilton):** Angel asks origin/destiny though v. 13 equates him with Yahweh (cf. Elijah 1 K 19:9). Hagar answers only the first question—knows recent history not future; suggests aimless wandering or reluctance to name Egypt. Before she speaks, angel knows name, position, mistress—episode under Yahweh’s control.  
**Quote:** “before Hagar speaks, the angel knows her name, her position, and the identity of her mistress. The impression given by all this is that the whole episode is under Yahweh’s control and vigilance.”  
**Locus:** L153–L155

### C-V1R6-17 — Return and accept abuse; faith/obedience; Trible’s “word of terror”
**Targets:** [[ishmael]], [[sarah]], [[hamilton-genesis-1-17-nicot]]  
**Claim (Hamilton):** Directive: return and accept ill-treatment (Hithpael *ʿānâ*); under mistress’s hand (*taḥaṯ yāḏeyhā* = authority). Possible comparison to Onesimus/Philemon. Cites Trible: “divine word of terror to an abused, yet courageous, woman.” Hagar offers no resistance—“a lady of faith and obedience.”  
**Quote:** “Knowing now that the situation may be even more tense than before, Hagar offers no resistance or rebuttal. She is a lady of faith and obedience.”

### C-V1R6-18 — Hagar alone among Genesis women receives innumerable-descendants promise
**Targets:** [[ishmael]], [[abraham]], [[covenant]], [[hamilton-genesis-1-17-nicot]]  
**Claim (Hamilton):** Angel promises Hagar innumerable descendants before she has one child. Many patriarchal men receive child/descendant promises; “Hagar is the only woman in Genesis who is honored with such a revelation. This sets her apart from the matriarchs of Israel.”  
**Quote:** “Hagar is the only woman in Genesis who is honored with such a revelation. This sets her apart from the matriarchs of Israel.”

### C-V1R6-19 — Ishmael name: Yahweh in etymology for El-name; not emendation
**Targets:** [[ishmael]], [[genesis]], [[hamilton-genesis-1-17-nicot]]  
**Claim (Hamilton):** Child to be named Ishmael—“Yahweh has been attentive to your humiliation.” Scholars puzzle that theophoric *ʾēl* is replaced by Yahweh in the etymology. Rejects Dahood’s NW Semitic redivision and Loretz’s redactional “El then angel of Yahweh” reconstruction. Parallels 1 Sam 1:20 (Samuel explained with Yahweh).  
**Quote:** “The OT provides at least one good instance of an X plus El name being explained with a phrase using the tetragrammaton: 1 Sam. 1:20…”  
**Locus:** L165–L171

### C-V1R6-20 — Wild ass of the steppe; hand against every man; *weʿal-penê* as defiance
**Targets:** [[ishmael]], [[hamilton-genesis-1-17-nicot]]  
**Claim (Hamilton):** Destiny oracle is “derogatory and derisive”: onager/wild ass of waste places (Job 39:5–8 etc.) → desert nomadic lifestyle. “Hand against every man…” = mutual belligerence. *weʿal-penê* not “before/east of” but “in defiance of, against” (cf. Exod 20:3 perhaps; Deut 21:16; Isa 65:3). Announcement needed so return to Sarai (v. 9) is not for nought—destiny protects pregnancy.  
**Quote:** “Ishmael is to be a wild ass of the steppe land. This designation is derogatory and derisive.”  
**Locus:** L173–L177

### C-V1R6-21 — Hagar names Yahweh *El Roi*; only mortal who names God
**Targets:** [[ishmael]], [[genesis]], [[hamilton-genesis-1-17-nicot]]  
**Claim (Hamilton):** Hagar revels in theophany more than content; no longer gloating over procreation. She does not “call upon the name” but *names* Yahweh who spoke with her—no other OT character does that. Name: “a God of seeing” (*ʾēl roʾî*)—objective genitive (“who may be seen”) or subjective (“who sees”) uncertain.  
**Quote:** “Hagar actually confers on deity a name. No other character in the OT, male or female, does that. … Her name for God is ‘a God of seeing’ (ʽēl roʾî).”  
**Locus:** L179

### C-V1R6-22 — “Seen the back of him who sees me” without Wellhausen-type emendation
**Targets:** [[genesis]], [[hamilton-genesis-1-17-nicot]]  
**Claim (Hamilton):** Rejects RSV/Wellhausen emendation (*halōm*→*ʾĕlōhîm*; insert “remained alive”). Prefers reading *ʾaḥarê* as “back” (cf. 2 Sam 2:23): “Have I really seen the back of him who sees me?”—parallels Moses seeing God’s back (Exod 33:23). Alternative: *ʾaḥarê* as “upon/with” → “looked upon the one who sees me.”  
**Quote:** “If the Heb. ʾaḥarê is taken as a noun meaning ‘back’… then the sentence reads: ‘Have I really seen the back of him who sees me?’ This idea of seeing the back of someone parallels in Exodus Moses who saw God’s back…”  
**Locus:** L181–L187

### C-V1R6-23 — Beer-lahai-roi: God as subject of seeing (grace), not Hagar’s status
**Targets:** [[ishmael]], [[genesis]], [[hamilton-genesis-1-17-nicot]]  
**Claim (Hamilton):** Well name means “the well belonging to the Living One who has seen me.” Focuses on God showing himself—not “whom I have seen.” Hagar is object not subject; commemorates graciousness to a pregnant woman in the wilderness. Located between Kadesh and Bered.  
**Quote:** “In effect, then, Beer-lahai-roi focuses on the graciousness of the God who manifested himself to a pregnant woman in the wilderness, rather than on any special status accorded to Hagar.”  
**Locus:** L191–L193

### C-V1R6-24 — Abram names Ishmael; Sarai absent; “for Abram” not “for them”
**Targets:** [[abraham]], [[sarah]], [[ishmael]], [[hamilton-genesis-1-17-nicot]]  
**Claim (Hamilton):** In 16:15–16 Hagar’s name thrice, Abram’s four times; Sarai conspicuously absent. Though Hagar was told to name the child, Abram names him—born in house and named by Abram → fully Abram’s son. Unlike Leah/Rachel naming maidservants’ sons, Sarai does not name Ishmael. Implication: Sarai’s “perhaps by her I shall reproduce” fails. Text stresses Hagar bore Abram (not the couple) a son.  
**Quote:** “Clearly Hagar bore Abram (not Abram and Sarai) a son (v. 15a). Abram named the son Hagar bore for him (not them) Ishmael (v. 15b).”  
**Locus:** L197–L199

### C-V1R6-26 — Source-critical vs traditional framing of Gen 17
**Targets:** [[genesis]], [[covenant]], [[documentary-hypothesis]], [[hamilton-genesis-1-17-nicot]], [[victor-hamilton]]  
**Claim (Hamilton):** Critics unanimously take Gen 17 as P’s Abrahamic covenant, later version beside J’s ch. 15—arguments: “God” not “Yahweh”; circumcision as priestly concern; verbal parallels with P Flood. Traditional view: ch. 17 reconfirms promises/oath; ≥11 years elapsed, Sarai still sterile, household rife with strife—one might wonder if promises still hold.  
**Quote:** “The critics unanimously accept Gen. 17 as P’s account of the covenant with Abraham, a later version to be placed besides J’s earlier account (ch. 15). … The traditional view argues that ch. 17 represents a reconfirmation of God’s covenant promises and oath to Abraham.”  
**Locus:** L262–L264

### C-V1R6-27 — Chapter structure: five divine speeches; demands ringed by promises
**Targets:** [[covenant]], [[abraham]], [[genesis]], [[hamilton-genesis-1-17-nicot]]  
**Claim (Hamilton):** Overall: speech (vv. 1–21) and action (vv. 22–27). Five speeches of God: I 1–2; II 3–8; III 9–14; IV 15–16; V 19–21. Abraham speaks twice (self, v. 17; briefly to God, v. 18). Speeches II, IV, V focus on blessing; I, III on expectations. Major action-speech on circumcision (9–14) ringed by promise speeches—demands interpreted within promises.  
**Quote:** “The major speech by God to Abraham about Abraham’s need to take appropriate action (w. 9-14) is ringed by speeches of God’s promises to Abraham (w. 3-8 and 15-21), showing that the demands of God must be interpreted within the context of the promises of God.”  
**Locus:** L266

### C-V1R6-28 — Thirteen silent years; *rāʾâ* vs *yāḏaʿ* (Exod 6:3) not primitive→refined
**Targets:** [[abraham]], [[genesis]], [[hamilton-genesis-1-17-nicot]]  
**Claim (Hamilton):** Thirteen silent years between 16:16 (86) and 17:1 (99); tense Hagar/Ishmael–Sarai years omitted. *wayyērāʾ* as in 12:7 etc. Against Rendtorff’s developmental scheme (visible appearance provisional; Moses more sophisticated *yāḏaʿ*): prefers customary stylistic idiom—*nôdaʿ* apposed not opposed to *nirʾah*; divine name additional designation after burning bush, not substitute.  
**Quote:** “Such an interpretation has the advantage of seeing the overlap in meaning and use of rā’â and yāḏaʿ, rather than forcing upon them differences they do not have.”  
**Locus:** L268–L274

### C-V1R6-29 — Walk before me and be blameless: ethical charge; accountability within unilateral covenant
**Targets:** [[abraham]], [[covenant]], [[hamilton-genesis-1-17-nicot]]  
**Claim (Hamilton):** Imperative has more ethical charge than earlier directives (leave; lift eyes; fear not, etc.). Though emphasis is on unilaterality of God’s covenant, healthy covenant relationship needs accountability by both partners. “Walk in front of” = service/devotion of faithful servant to king (human or divine). *tāmîm*: for Noah accomplished fact (6:9); for Abraham a goal. LXX *ámemptos* for Abram vs *téleios* for Noah; also ritual “unblemished”; may carry “transparent/candid” (Josh 24:14).  
**Quote:** “Although the emphasis is on the unilaterality of God’s covenant with Abraham, any covenant relationship, if it is to be healthy, needs accountability by both partners.”  
**Locus:** L276–L280

### C-V1R6-30 — El Shaddai: etymologies; posterity association in Genesis
**Targets:** [[abraham]], [[genesis]], [[hamilton-genesis-1-17-nicot]]  
**Claim (Hamilton):** El Shaddai 48× OT (Job 31× without El). Modern “God Almighty” via LXX *pantokrátōr* / Vulg *omnipotens*. Etymology proposals: *še* + *day* “sufficient” (Aquila/Symm. *hikanós*); *šāḏaḏ* destroy/overpower (Isa 13:6 wordplay); *śāḏeh* “El of the plain”; “breast”→“mountain” (El of the mountain); *bêl sadê* / Amurru “Lord of the steppe.” In Genesis always with Jacob except here; five of six times followed by posterity promise; thrice *bāraḵ*.  
**Quote:** “In five of the six places in Genesis where El Shaddai is used, the name is followed by the promise of posterity.”  
**Locus:** L282–L288

### C-V1R6-31 — *berît* density in ch. 17 vs ch. 15; structure 17:1–2 // 12:1–2
**Targets:** [[covenant]], [[abraham]], [[genesis]], [[hamilton-genesis-1-17-nicot]]  
**Claim (Hamilton):** Structure of 17:1–2 same as 12:1–2: imperative(s) + imperfects of intention. “Covenant” once in ch. 15 (v. 18); thirteen times in ch. 17 (2, 4, 7×2, 9, 10, 11, 13×2, 14, 19×2, 21). First four and last three in promissory speeches; middle six in circumcision speech.  
**Quote:** “Whereas it occurred but once in ch. 15 (v. 18), in ch. 17 it occurs thirteen times…”  
**Locus:** L290

### C-V1R6-32 — Abram matures: complaint (15) → obeisance (17); order of son vs multitude reversed
**Targets:** [[abraham]], [[covenant]], [[isaac]], [[hamilton-genesis-1-17-nicot]]  
**Claim (Hamilton):** Prostration from theophany + word, not theophany alone. Contrast ch. 15 response (complaint 15:2–3) with obeisance here—Abram mellowing/maturing. Ch. 15: specific son (15:4) then numerous progeny (15:5); ch. 17: numerous progeny (17:2, 4) then specific son (17:16).  
**Quote:** “Abraham’s reaction here contrasts with his earlier reaction when he received covenantal promises. There his response was a complaint (15:2—3). Here it is obeisance. Abram is mellowing; he is maturing.”  
**Locus:** L294

### C-V1R6-33 — Abram → Abraham: father of host of nations; universal vs circumcision particular
**Targets:** [[abraham]], [[covenant]], [[circumcision]], [[hamilton-genesis-1-17-nicot]]  
**Claim (Hamilton):** First individual name *change* in Genesis. Abram ≈ “exalted (as to) father” / “the father is exalted.” Abraham not literally *ʾaḇ hamôn* but phonemic similarity; Ugaritic -h- insertion analogies. New name universalizes experience with God; circumcision later particularizes (father of Israelites). He is father of many *gōyim*, not many *yehûḏîm*.  
**Quote:** “One significance of the patriarch’s new name is that it universalizes Abraham’s experience with God. This point contrasts with the later emphasis in the chapter on circumcision, which particularizes Abraham’s relationship with God. … He is to be the father of many gōyim, not many yehûḏîm.”  
**Locus:** L296–L302

### C-V1R6-34 — Fertility, kings, eternal covenant language
**Targets:** [[abraham]], [[covenant]], [[isaac]], [[hamilton-genesis-1-17-nicot]]  
**Claim (Hamilton):** *pārâ* recalls creation/Noah/later Ishmael/Jacob. Promise includes kings (*melāḵîm*). Hiphil *qûm* “maintain”: initiate, maintain, fulfill. *ʿôlām* thrice of covenant (7, 13, 19) and land permanent (v. 8); Kaiser: *ʿôlām* adds to already-strong perpetuity of covenant.

### C-V1R6-35 — **Hamilton’s core view: Gen 15 and 17 one covenant; eternal stress preserves unilaterality**
**Targets:** [[covenant]], [[abraham]], [[genesis]], [[documentary-hypothesis]], [[hamilton-genesis-1-17-nicot]], [[victor-hamilton]]  
**Claim (Hamilton):** *Eternal* present in ch. 17, absent in ch. 15, is no accident. In the chapter with ≥four stipulations (walk before me; be blameless; keep my covenant; circumcise), thrice calling the covenant eternal emphasizes it has **not** shifted from ch. 15’s unilateral emphasis to a bilateral pact. Expectations do not become grounds for establishment/authentication; covenant remains God’s personal commitment binding himself to open-ended promise.  
**Quote:** “This repetition of eternal emphasizes that God’s covenant with Abraham has not suddenly shifted away from the unilateral emphasis of ch. 15 to a bilateral pact here in ch. 17. ### C-V1R6-48 — NT Appropriation: circumcision spiritualized; Rom 4 seal; not simply baptism replacement
**Targets:** [[circumcision]], [[covenant]], [[abraham]], [[hamilton-genesis-1-17-nicot]]  
**Claim (Hamilton):** NT examples of circumcised persons: Jesus (Luke 2:21), John (Luke 1:59–60), Paul (Phil 3:5), Timothy. Also “spiritual” circumcision (Phil 3:3; Col 2:11–13; Rom 2:28–29). 1 Cor 7:19; Gal 5:6: neither circumcision nor uncircumcision decisive. Paul’s misgivings target contemporary distortion making rite end-in-itself, not OT institution (God’s idea); Acts 15 removes requirement for church membership; Gal heat (5:2, 6; 6:12–15). **Rom 4:9–12:** circumcision a sign/seal of righteousness already given; circumcised and uncircumcised believers claim Abraham as father. OT already initiates internalization: heart circumcision (Lev 26:41; Deut 10:16; 30:6; Jer 4:4; Ezek 44:7, 9); ear (Jer 6:10). Functional equation with infant baptism common among Christians, but NT never makes that equation; only Col 2:8–12 pairs them—baptism as Christian circumcision *made without hands* (*acheiropoiḗtos* = God’s doing); does not settle infant baptism debate. Absence of “baptism replaces circumcision” in Acts 15 suggests early church did not envision baptism as simple supplanter.  
**Quote:** “The value in circumcision is that it was, on Abraham’s part, a sign or seal of the righteousness God has already given him (Rom. 4:9-12).”  
**Locus:** L529–L543

## Cross-cutting synthesis notes (for integrator; still Hamilton-attributed)

1. **One covenant (15 + 17):** Hamilton rejects treating 17 as a different bilateral “P” covenant that replaces unilateral 15; *eternal* language + Hiphil *qûm* (not *kāraṯ*) frame reaffirmation/maintenance within God’s unilateral commitment, with human accountability subsidiary (C-V1R6-26, 35, 45).  
2. **Hagar’s theological dignity:** only Genesis woman with innumerable-seed oracle; only mortal who names God (*El Roi*); faith-return under abuse; yet naming of Ishmael and “for Abram” language deny Sarai’s reproductive claim and exclude Hagar from naming (C-V1R6-18, 21, 24).  
3. **Ishmael:** blessed, nationed, circumcised, not covenant-heir; divine sovereignty not moral disqualification (C-V1R6-45, 47).  
4. **Circumcision:** confirmation/identity *ʾôṯ* and amen parallel to 15:6 faith; *kareth* for omission; NT spiritual reading continuous with OT heart circumcision; Rom 4 seal of prior righteousness (C-V1R6-38, 40, 48).  
5. **Documentary Hypothesis footprint in-range:** critical consensus on P (17) vs J (15) stated and contrasted with traditional reconfirmation reading (C-V1R6-26); Van Seters dating caution on surrogacy customs (C-V1R6-04); Rendtorff on revelation verbs engaged and declined (C-V1R6-28).
